title: Buddy Bolden's training, the church and the Bass sisters
summary: Disputes over whether Bolden read, church influence on early jazz, and Bolden's wife's recollections.

story.theme_name: Church, faith and religion in a musician's life
story.community_name: Church, faith and jazz: the sacred and the secular

blocks.x: No. Was Buddy Bolden a reader? Did anyone know?
There's always a dispute on that. He probably did. It was a fellow Jones that talks about how he even mentioned Buddy Bolden's teacher. Lewis Jones.
It's interesting because someone mentioned that Bolden used to get his inspiration from the church. That is, he'd hear the spirituals in the church and anything that, any jazz influence.

It was mainly people, I'm not sure just who it was, it was probably Bud Scott and Kid Ori. I know Kid Ori in print or in some interview at least that we have is told about Bolden being inspired by the spirituals coming out of the church. Which in this,
this aspect of the origins of jazz is completely a non-reading that call response pattern is completely outside the reading tradition and that plays a big part in it of course.

I think it was Bud Scott too told me in California, that was 1940 when I talked to him in 39, maybe 1940 that winter I was there. Bolden used to take these twin sisters Nora and Dora Bass to a church, it was a Baptist church supposedly, which doesn't always have the best music, usually some of the, well as you'd call them, sanctified churches or things like Church of God and Christ that have more dancing and instrumental music in them than the Baptists usually. But, anyway, speaking of the Bass sisters, I talked to the one that married, I talked to both of them once, but the one that married Bolden says that he never made a nickel was the expression that she used outside of music that every cent he ever made was only for music that he did wasn't a barber as far as she knew. He might have done a little barbering at that as far as we know, at least they would hang out around a barber shop, you know, it was sort of a customary place a lot of musicians in all cities used to do that.
Most musicians at that time too were now doing the music full-time, were they?

No, a lot of them didn't. Very few of them probably did. Well, anyway, his wife also said that he had the best training that his mother could have gotten him, that she got him the best teachers and the best training he could get. So he probably could read music but probably didn't most of the time. well, Mineta is told too that on the bandstand he would have a pile of music there sometimes. He mentions the different pieces he played like some of the later tunes like say Ida, Sweet as Apple Cider and I think Moon Winks are several things that came out around the early 20s in the early 1900s, 1900 to 1906 period. So he probably did play some of those things maybe not from music on the stand either but was able to read.
